title: Arbitrary-phase CZ gate and remote readout across spatially separated superconducting nodes
authors: Anatoly Kulikov, Josua D. Schär, Alonso Hernández-Antón, Aleksandr Grigorev
abstract: Establishing a complete set of gates across spatially separated quantum nodes is fundamental for distributed quantum computation and communication networks. One of the approaches to do so consists of employing a superconducting device as a universal quantum node that is capable of storing and processing quantum information, and traveling microwave photons as means of communication. In this work, we realize an entangling gate across a primitive two-node superconducting circuit QED network consisting of two dilution cryostats, A and B, connected via a 30-m-long cryogenic quantum link. We perform a bidirectional photon transfer protocol, where a microwave photon emitted by the communication qubit at A acquires a conditional phase based on the state of qubit B. We vary the communication photon frequency, hence tuning the conditional phase acquired during the reflection off the remote node, effectively implementing an arbitrary-phase CZ gate. We use this entangling operation to perform single-shot readout of the qubit in node B from node A. An interesting feature of our scheme is that it does not require precise synchronization of the active node with the remote node; in particular, remote readout can be performed without any active participation by the remote node. These protocols add to the quantum communication toolbox with superconducting circuits and provide a way of realizing basic distributed quantum computing operations.
summary: This paper demonstrates a method to implement an arbitrary-phase CZ gate and perform remote readout between two physically separated superconducting quantum nodes. This is achieved by sending microwave photons across a long cryogenic link, where the photon acquires a state-dependent phase upon reflection. The key breakthrough is the ability to tune this phase without active participation from the remote node, advancing distributed quantum computing capabilities.
main_problem: The core challenge is establishing a complete set of quantum gates across spatially separated quantum nodes for distributed quantum computation and communication.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated an arbitrary-phase CZ gate and remote single-shot readout using a bidirectional photon transfer protocol across superconducting nodes.
method: The protocol relies on tuning the conditional phase acquired by a microwave photon reflected off a remote qubit by varying the photon's frequency detuning.
model_or_system: The system uses a two-node superconducting circuit QED network (A and B) connected by a 30-m cryogenic link, employing frequency-tunable transmon qubits.
key_observables: Conditional phase (Delta_phi), readout fidelity, and the population of the remote qubit.
important_parameters: Photon detuning (delta_omega), coupling strength (tilde_g), and the required number of repetitions for error correction.
main_assumptions: The primary sources of infidelity are attributed to microwave components, and the variable-frequency emission method is presented as a practical first-order solution.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the bidirectional photon transfer protocol, the dependence of the conditional phase on detuning, and the improvement of readout fidelity using error correction techniques like majority voting and weighted decoding.
paper_structure: The work progresses by first establishing the basic protocol for the CZ gate, then detailing the technique for tuning the conditional phase via variable-frequency emission, and finally demonstrating robust remote readout using error correction codes.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, hardware-based realization of quantum networking primitives (entangling gates and remote measurement) using superconducting circuits, which is highly relevant for quantum information theorists designing network protocols.
